[8] These cranes are part of the Pacific Flyway Population which breeds in areas including the Alaska Peninsula and the Cook Inlet region. [3, 7] Their migration route takes them south along the coast to their wintering grounds in California's Central Valley. [2, 3, 7] Sightings occurred in Anchor Point and Homer, which are located along the southern Kenai Peninsula, adjacent to Cook Inlet. [8] <2> To manage the local elk population, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, in partnership with the Wyoming Game and Fish Department, announced new hunting regulations for the National Elk Refuge for the fall 2023 season. Key changes included instituting a daily limit of one elk tag per hunter to improve safety. Additionally, youth hunting opportunities were expanded, with two, two-day "Youth Only Elk Hunts" scheduled over the 2023 Thanksgiving weekend. Other changes for the season included a new Hunting Permit Review process and updates to how disabled hunter parking permits are reserved. <3> A World Economic Forum article highlighted that record-breaking global temperatures in September 2023 are a contributing factor to widespread species migration. [2] Data from the Copernicus Climate Change Service confirmed that September 2023 was the warmest September on record, with a global average surface air temperature 0.93°C above the 1991-2020 average, making it the most anomalously warm month in its dataset. [1, 4] The Forum's report, citing researchers at the University of Southern California, noted that approximately half of all species are on the move, including animals like moose, bears, frogs, and squirrels. [2] These species are generally migrating to cooler environments, which predominantly means moving further north and to higher elevations, to escape rising temperatures. [2] <4> An article by the National Environmental Education Foundation (NEEF), published on October 4, 2023, details how climate change is altering the habits and migration patterns of various North American species. [1] The report explains that warmer temperatures, which cause plants to bloom earlier or expand their range, disrupt ecosystems. [1] As specific examples, the article cites that warmer temperatures late in the year have delayed the start of the fall caribou migration. [1] Additionally, as ocean waters warm, the distribution of many marine species is shifting, which can disrupt the entire food web because different species respond to these changes at different rates. [1] <5> A report from the National Environmental Education Foundation (NEEF), published on October 4, 2023, details how climate change is altering the migration patterns and habits of various North American species. The report specifies that over the last 30 years, warmer temperatures have delayed the start of the caribou migration. It also notes that shifts in temperature and precipitation are creating a 'mismatch' between predator and prey species, as they respond differently to these climate-driven changes. <6> On August 1, 2023, BirdCast, a collaborative project by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and Colorado State University, launched its suite of migration tools for the fall 2023 season. [1] The project provides the public with migration forecasts and live maps to track avian movements in near-real-time. [1] A Migration Dashboard is also available for users to compare migration data in their local county and state with historical averages. [1] <7> The annual fall bird migration across the United States was officially noted as underway for the 2023 season on August 1, 2023, by BirdCast, a project by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and Colorado State University. This massive natural event involves billions of birds. Research based on weather radar data indicates that an average of 4.7 billion birds leave the U.S. over its southern border for the tropics each autumn, while another 4 billion birds move south from Canada into the U.S. The migration period lasts from August through November, with some early movements beginning as soon as mid-June for certain species. Peak migration activity typically occurs during September and October. Many species, including songbirds, travel at night, using the moon and stars for navigation. To protect these birds from disorientation caused by light pollution, conservation initiatives like "Lights Out" advocate for turning off non-essential lights at night during the migration months. <8> A multi-year collaborative study by Portland State University (PSU) and the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife (ODFW) has produced a statewide map of crucial wildlife corridors. The project, named the Oregon Connectivity Assessment and Mapping Project (OCAMP), identifies critical habitat connectivity areas for 54 species, including both large mammals and smaller animals like butterflies, to help preserve biodiversity. The resulting interactive "Priority Wildlife Connectivity Areas Map" was developed to inform the placement of wildlife crossings, guide land use planning, and help reduce vehicle collisions on high-traffic routes. The project, which began in 2019 and was completed in 2022, is now in its implementation phase. State and local agencies, including the Oregon Department of Transportation (ODOT) and the Department of Land Conservation and Development, are expected to utilize the map to guide new developments and mitigate the impact of highways on wildlife. <9> The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) has revised its regulations under Section 10(j) of the Endangered Species Act to grant more flexibility for the introduction of experimental populations of listed species outside of their historical ranges. This final rule, which was announced on July 3, 2023, and became effective on August 2, 2023, is a response to the growing impacts of climate change and invasive species, which are causing habitats within species’ historical ranges to become unsuitable. The previous regulations generally restricted such introductions to a species' historical range except under extreme circumstances. The updated rule allows the FWS to proactively establish populations in new, suitable habitats to prevent extinctions and aid in the recovery of imperiled species. The FWS stated that any decision to establish an experimental population must still be based on the best available science and that potential adverse effects on the ecosystem will be considered. <10> A significant toxic algal bloom of Pseudo-nitzschia occurred along the Southern California coast in June 2023, resulting in the deaths and sickness of hundreds of marine animals due to domoic acid poisoning. The Channel Islands Marine and Wildlife Institute reported fielding over 300 daily reports of distressed marine mammals. By late June, it was estimated that over 1,000 sea lions had been sickened or died, and the death toll for dolphins had reached approximately 100. The crisis prompted a large-scale response from marine wildlife stranding networks, with rescue centers becoming overwhelmed by the number of affected animals. In response to the high concentrations of the neurotoxin, public health officials issued warnings, advising beachgoers to keep their distance from oddly behaving marine mammals and cautioning against the consumption of sport-harvested shellfish from affected counties.

Ahead of the hearing, the National Parks Conservation Association (NPCA) submitted a formal position to the committee. [4, 5] The project, with a total estimated cost of $37.4 million, will be supplemented by state funds and contributions from various partners. [4] It includes the construction of one wildlife overpass, five underpasses, and associated fencing. [4] This initiative aims to improve habitat connectivity and is expected to reduce wildlife-vehicle collisions by 80-90%. [4] The primary beneficiaries will be the Wyoming Range and Uinta mule deer herds, as well as the Carter Lease pronghorn herd, which frequently cross this corridor. [4] The grant to Wyoming was a significant portion, over 20%, of the roughly $112 million awarded nationwide in the program's first funding cycle. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The Sublette Pronghorn Herd undertakes a crucial long-distance fall migration, one of the longest for any land mammal in the lower 48 states, to survive harsh high-elevation winters in Wyoming. [4, 8] The herd travels from summer ranges in areas like the Jackson Hole, Bondurant, and the foothills of the Wyoming Range to wintering grounds near Pinedale, the Green River Valley, and Rock Springs. [8, 9] Facing increasing threats from development and habitat fragmentation, the Wyoming Game and Fish Commission unanimously voted on March 12, 2024, to advance the formal designation and protection of this vital migration corridor. [4] This step initiates further research and a 'biological risk assessment' before a final decision is made by the governor. [4] <2> In response to growing threats from development, including subdivisions and energy projects, a significant push to protect the 'Path of the Pronghorn' migration corridor in western Wyoming is underway. After a 2023 threat evaluation by the Wyoming Game and Fish Department deemed the critical route at 'high risk' of being lost, and following a multi-year stall in state-level protections due to political pressures, conservation advocates intensified their efforts. Bolstered by strong public backing, with about 90% of comments favoring protection, the campaign saw a major development on March 12, 2024. On that day, the Wyoming Game and Fish Commission voted unanimously to advance the designation process for the corridor, a key step toward securing its future. The process continues, with a final vote by the commission on whether to recommend formal designation to the governor anticipated in the latter half of 2025. <3> Research led by scientists from the University of Wyoming and the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior has shown that migrating animals refine their routes through experience as they age. [1, 3] The study, published on March 4, 2024, in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, tracked over 250 white storks from 2013 to 2020. [3, 4] It was found that individual storks incrementally straightened their spring migration paths to find more direct routes to their summer breeding grounds. [1, 3] While younger birds focused on energy-efficient exploration and information gathering, older, more experienced birds moved more quickly and directly. [4] This indicates that experiential learning is a significant factor in successful migration, complementing the roles of genetics and social learning. [1, 3] <4> A record number of sandhill cranes were observed in Nebraska during the early stages of the 2024 annual migration count conducted by the Crane Trust. The count on February 14, 2024, estimated 38,000 sandhill cranes, the highest number ever recorded for the first week of the aerial survey which began in 1998. This initial count was significantly higher than the typical 6,000 to 8,000 cranes seen in the first week. By February 24, 2024, the number had surged to an estimated 122,700, which was also a record for the second week of the count and about five times the average for that period. Wildlife biologist Bethany Ostrom noted that mild winter temperatures were a likely cause for the unusually high early arrival numbers. <5> In a landmark, first-ever "State of the World’s Migratory Species" report, the United Nations has revealed that nearly half (44%) of the world's migratory species are experiencing population declines. The report, launched by the UN's Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS), also found that more than one-fifth (22%) of these species are threatened with extinction. The assessment, released during a UN wildlife conference in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, identified overexploitation—such as unsustainable hunting and fishing—and habitat loss from human activities as the two greatest threats to these animals. It was noted that three out of four CMS-listed species are impacted by habitat loss, and seven out of ten are affected by overexploitation. The report also highlighted the growing risk for species not listed under the convention and emphasized that climate change, pollution, and invasive species are also having profound impacts. <6> A landmark United Nations report, titled the 'State of the World's Migratory Species', has revealed that nearly half (44%) of the world's migratory species are experiencing population declines, with more than one-fifth (22%) threatened with extinction. The report, the first of its kind from the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS), was launched on February 12, 2024, at a UN wildlife conservation conference in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. It identifies overexploitation and habitat loss from human activity as the two greatest threats to these species. The report also underscores the profound impact of climate change, which can amplify other threats and disrupt migratory patterns. A specific example highlighted is the situation in Alaska, where rising temperatures are causing a dangerous mismatch between the timing of insect emergence and the chick-rearing of shorebirds, which depend on them for food. This phenological mismatch threatens the growth and survival of shorebird chicks. <7> New data for the 2023-2024 overwintering season revealed a 59% decrease in the eastern monarch butterfly population in Mexico's forests. [1] The annual survey, announced on February 7, 2024, by the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) and partners, found that the butterflies occupied only 2.2 acres (0.9 hectares), down from 5.5 acres (2.21 hectares) the previous year. [1, 2, 4, 5] This marks the second-smallest area occupied by the colonies since monitoring began in 1993, with the lowest recorded in the 2013-2014 season. [1, 5] Scientists attribute the sharp decline to climate variations, specifically high temperatures and drought conditions in the monarchs' breeding grounds in the United States and Canada, which reduced the availability of milkweed, the sole plant where monarchs lay their eggs. [1, 5, 7] <8> In a significant ecological development, gray wolves were reintroduced to Colorado in late 2023, fulfilling a voter-mandated initiative. On December 18, 2023, Colorado Parks and Wildlife (CPW) began the historic release of ten gray wolves sourced from Oregon into public lands in Grand and Summit counties. This action was the result of Proposition 114, a state statute passed on November 3, 2020, which directed the CPW Commission to re-establish a permanent, self-sustaining wolf population on the Western Slope. The initiative aims to restore the state's natural ecosystem balance, with advocates celebrating the return of the apex predator. However, the reintroduction has been met with concern from some ranchers regarding potential conflicts with livestock, a concern the state has addressed by creating a compensation program for any livestock losses. The reintroduction plan was approved by the CPW Commission in May 2023, and a final rule establishing an experimental population was made effective on December 8, 2023, providing management flexibility. News of the reintroduction and the various perspectives surrounding it were reported by outlets including CNN 10 in early April 2024.

Prediction target period: from 2024-06-09 to 2024-08-25. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> World Fish Migration Day, an international event held every two years, was celebrated in the Gulf of Maine region and globally on May 25, 2024, with the theme 'Free Flow'. The celebration aimed to raise awareness about the critical importance of free-flowing rivers for migratory fish. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's Gulf of Maine Coastal Program participated by highlighting its collaborative efforts to remove barriers to fish passage. These efforts are vital for the life cycles of diadromous, or 'sea run,' fish such as Atlantic salmon, alewife, and American shad, which migrate between freshwater and the ocean. Organizations like NOAA also used the day to feature their nationwide projects aimed at restoring access to habitats for these species. <2> President Biden signed the Migratory Birds of the Americas Conservation Enhancements Act of 2023 into law on April 24, 2024. [2, 3, 4] This bipartisan legislation reauthorizes the Neotropical Migratory Bird Conservation Act (NMBCA), a grant program dedicated to funding bird research and habitat restoration projects throughout the Western Hemisphere. [1, 2] A key enhancement of the new law is the reduction of the cost-sharing requirement for partner organizations from a 3-to-1 to a 2-to-1 match, a change intended to boost participation and support for the conservation of over 350 migratory bird species. [1] Since 2002, the NMBCA has supported over 700 projects across 35 countries, conserving more than 5 million acres of habitat. [1] <3> The fall migration of the eastern monarch butterfly is being significantly impacted by climate change, particularly unseasonably warm temperatures, which are causing delays in their journey south. [1, 2, 8] Research indicates that from 1992 to 2020, migration timing shifted later by 16 to 19 days. [3] This warming trend allows some monarchs to persist farther north than their traditional overwintering sites in Mexico, with an increasing number remaining in the southern and coastal U.S. for the winter, including along the Gulf Coast. [6, 12] While warmer conditions can be associated with larger roosts, studies of citizen-scientist data have documented a dramatic decline in the size of these migratory roosts over the last two decades, especially in southern regions like Texas. [13, 14] The presence of monarchs along the Florida Gulf Coast is a notable part of the migration, as it's a final stop before their flight over the Gulf of Mexico. [12] However, there is a conflict in findings, as some research suggests the timing of migration has remained relatively unchanged, even while noting that the migratory flyway has become warmer. [14] This shift also raises conservation concerns, as non-migratory monarchs have shown higher rates of parasite infection. [6] <4> In an April 12, 2024, report, part of a 14-week 'Striper Migration Report' video series by On The Water magazine, the spring migration of striped bass in the Hudson River and New York City area was detailed. The report, corresponding to the third week of the series, featured insights from Joe Albanese of the Hudson River Fisherman’s Association. Key topics included the status of the spawning run in the Hudson, the critical role of river herring and bunker as primary food sources for the bass, and methods for differentiating between local resident stripers and the larger migratory fish. The series tracks the entire migration from Chesapeake Bay, where spawning conditions were reported to be nearing their peak, to their eventual destination in Maine. <5> The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), in collaboration with the University of Wyoming and the Corridor Mapping Team, released the fourth volume of 'Ungulate Migrations of the Western United States' on April 11, 2024. [2, 3, 4] This volume expands the series with detailed maps of 33 migration routes for mule deer, pronghorn, and elk, including 31 new herds and updates to two previously documented ones. [1, 2] The report covers nine western states: Arizona, California, Colorado, New Mexico, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming, marking the first inclusion of data from Oregon and Colorado. [2, 3] The maps serve as a critical tool for wildlife managers, policymakers, conservation groups, and developers, aiming to conserve crucial habitats and inform policy on renewable energy development and wildlife disease management. [1, 2, 3, 4] <6> The Sublette Pronghorn Herd undertakes a crucial long-distance fall migration, one of the longest for any land mammal in the lower 48 states, to survive harsh high-elevation winters in Wyoming. [4, 8] The herd travels from summer ranges in areas like the Jackson Hole, Bondurant, and the foothills of the Wyoming Range to wintering grounds near Pinedale, the Green River Valley, and Rock Springs. [8, 9] Facing increasing threats from development and habitat fragmentation, the Wyoming Game and Fish Commission unanimously voted on March 12, 2024, to advance the formal designation and protection of this vital migration corridor. [4] This step initiates further research and a 'biological risk assessment' before a final decision is made by the governor. [4] <7> In response to growing threats from development, including subdivisions and energy projects, a significant push to protect the 'Path of the Pronghorn' migration corridor in western Wyoming is underway. After a 2023 threat evaluation by the Wyoming Game and Fish Department deemed the critical route at 'high risk' of being lost, and following a multi-year stall in state-level protections due to political pressures, conservation advocates intensified their efforts. Bolstered by strong public backing, with about 90% of comments favoring protection, the campaign saw a major development on March 12, 2024. On that day, the Wyoming Game and Fish Commission voted unanimously to advance the designation process for the corridor, a key step toward securing its future. The process continues, with a final vote by the commission on whether to recommend formal designation to the governor anticipated in the latter half of 2025. <8> Research led by scientists from the University of Wyoming and the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior has shown that migrating animals refine their routes through experience as they age. [1, 3] The study, published on March 4, 2024, in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, tracked over 250 white storks from 2013 to 2020. [3, 4] It was found that individual storks incrementally straightened their spring migration paths to find more direct routes to their summer breeding grounds. [1, 3] While younger birds focused on energy-efficient exploration and information gathering, older, more experienced birds moved more quickly and directly. [4] This indicates that experiential learning is a significant factor in successful migration, complementing the roles of genetics and social learning. [1, 3] <9> Multiple events across the United States were held to celebrate World Migratory Bird Day on May 11, 2024, which centered on the theme "Protect Insects, Protect Birds." This theme highlighted the critical role insects play as a vital food source for migratory birds and the threats to their populations from pesticides and habitat loss. The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service and other organizations hosted numerous events, including guided bird walks, festivals, educational activities, and bird counts. Confirmed events took place in Wisconsin at Horicon National Wildlife Refuge and Trempealeau National Wildlife Refuge; in Indiana at Muscatatuck National Wildlife Refuge; in West Virginia at the National Conservation Training Center and Canaan Valley National Wildlife Refuge; a joint event for Iowa and Nebraska at DeSoto and Boyer Chute National Wildlife Refuges; and in Minnesota at Sherburne National Wildlife Refuge. Additional local events were also held in states like Iowa and Minnesota on May 11th. <10> A record number of sandhill cranes were observed in Nebraska during the early stages of the 2024 annual migration count conducted by the Crane Trust. The count on February 14, 2024, estimated 38,000 sandhill cranes, the highest number ever recorded for the first week of the aerial survey which began in 1998. This initial count was significantly higher than the typical 6,000 to 8,000 cranes seen in the first week. By February 24, 2024, the number had surged to an estimated 122,700, which was also a record for the second week of the count and about five times the average for that period. Wildlife biologist Bethany Ostrom noted that mild winter temperatures were a likely cause for the unusually high early arrival numbers.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The 35th annual Festival of the Cranes is scheduled to occur from December 11-15, 2024, at the Bosque del Apache National Wildlife Refuge in New Mexico. [1, 3] This event celebrates the yearly fall migration of tens of thousands of Sandhill Cranes, which journey from their northern breeding grounds in the United States and Canada to winter in the Middle Rio Grande Valley. [2] In addition to the cranes, the refuge also hosts a substantial number of other migratory birds, including an estimated 70,000 snow geese and over 40,000 ducks representing at least 14 species. [5] <2> The 'Lights Out, Texas!' campaign, facilitated by Audubon Texas and its partners, encourages businesses and residents to turn off non-essential lights from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. to protect the nearly two billion birds that migrate through the state. The effort aims to prevent disorientation and fatal collisions caused by light pollution. The full fall migration period runs from August 15 to November 30, with a designated peak period from September 5 to October 29, during which turning off lights is most critical. The program was initially launched in 2017 by Houston Audubon following a significant bird collision event and has since expanded into a statewide initiative with numerous partners. <3> The 2024 Bristol Bay sockeye salmon season began with an Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) preseason forecast of approximately 39 million fish. [4, 9, 12] By early July, as the run was underway, University of Washington researchers revised their forecast upward to 53.2 million, citing in-season data. [3] The preliminary post-season summary from ADF&G, released September 17, 2024, reported the actual inshore sockeye run was 51.6 million fish. [1, 2] This total was 36% above the initial state forecast and marked the tenth consecutive year the run exceeded 50 million fish. [1, 5] The commercial harvest was 31.6 million sockeye, which was 26% above the preseason forecast. [1] Despite the strong run size, the average weight of the sockeye was the smallest on record at 4.53 pounds. [1, 11] This, combined with other market factors, contributed to a preliminary ex-vessel value of $128.1 million for all salmon species, 34% below the 20-year average. [1, 15] <4> The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) has announced prime viewing locations within national wildlife refuges for the fall monarch butterfly migration. The annual migration, a journey that can span 3,000 miles, begins in late August as millions of monarchs head to warmer climates for the winter. An FWS article published on September 12, 2024, specifically highlighted several refuges. Key among them is the Balcones Canyonlands National Wildlife Refuge in Texas, which offers views of thousands of passing monarchs daily during late September and early October. Another premier location is the Eastern Shore of Virginia National Wildlife Refuge, situated on a major migration route, with the best viewing times from early September through October. <5> The 2024 fall migration of monarch butterflies is being tracked by Journey North, with September reports showing a mix of ongoing northern sightings and significant concerns from scientists. The overwintering population from the 2023-2024 season saw a dramatic 59% decrease, the second lowest on record, largely attributed to habitat loss and climate change factors such as drought and high temperatures impacting milkweed availability. This has led to predictions of fewer monarchs being visible during the fall migration. The migration, which typically runs from late August through October, has seen some delays in arrival to overwintering sites in Mexico. While some late-season egg and larva sightings were reported in northern areas like Wisconsin and Pennsylvania in early September, these have been tailing off. There are conflicting viewpoints on the long-term status of the monarch population; while the recent numbers are alarming to many conservationists, some scientists argue that the overall population remains resilient and that conservation efforts should be carefully considered to avoid unintended harm. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is re-evaluating the monarch's status for potential listing under the Endangered Species Act by the end of 2024. <6> The fall bird migration season began, prompting BirdCast, a project by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and Colorado State University, to issue migration alerts. A 'high alert' was specifically announced for the Chicago region for the nights of Thursday, September 5, and Friday, September 6, 2024. It was anticipated that hundreds of millions of birds would be migrating across the country, with the intensity over Chicago predicted to be in the range of 30,000 birds per kilometer. To protect the migrating birds, which are drawn to and disoriented by bright lights, citizens and building managers were advised to turn off non-essential lighting between 11 p.m. and 6 a.m. <7> The Wyoming Game and Fish Department (WGFD) released its 2024 fall hunting forecast on August 28, 2024, providing status updates on various big game herds. The forecast confirmed that the Sublette pronghorn herd experienced a significant decline, attributed to the severe winter of 2022-2023 and an outbreak of the bacterial disease Mycoplasma bovis. This outbreak, which causes a deadly respiratory illness, compounded the fatalities from the harsh winter conditions. As a result of the population decline, Hunt Area 85, which is part of the Sublette herd's range, remained closed for the 2024 season to support the herd's recovery. The WGFD will continue to monitor the herd to determine when hunting can be safely reauthorized. The report also noted that mule deer populations are recovering from the same severe winter. <8> The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) released its "Status and Harvests of Sandhill Cranes, 2024" report, detailing population data for several groups of sandhill cranes in North America. The report confirms that the spring 2024 abundance estimate for the Mid-Continent Population (MCP) in the Central Platte River Valley (CPRV) of Nebraska was 420,840 birds. This figure represents a 67% decrease from the 2023 estimate of 1,259,199. The aerial survey contributing to this estimate was conducted on March 22, 2024. Despite this significant one-year drop, the photo-corrected three-year average (2022-2024) for the CPRV remains at 788,505, which is well above the established population objective range of 350,000–475,000 cranes. The report also provides status and harvest information for the Rocky Mountain, Lower Colorado River Valley, and Eastern populations, noting that the MCP is the most abundant of all North American crane populations. <9> The Idaho Fish and Game (IDFG) provided an update on the 2024 fall salmon runs, noting that early counts suggest returns for both Chinook and coho will be higher than preseason forecasts. [2, 3] The fall Chinook run is now predicted to be around 35,000 fish, a significant increase from the initial 24,000 forecast. [3] Similarly, the coho run is expected to reach approximately 24,000 fish, well above the 14,000 forecasted. [2, 3] The fall Chinook season opened on August 18, 2024, for the Snake, Salmon, and most of the Clearwater rivers. [2, 4] The coho salmon season was scheduled to begin on September 1, 2024, in the Snake River and much of the Clearwater River basin. [2, 3] High counts at Bonneville Dam—the most ever recorded for the period of August 1 through August 28—supported the optimistic outlook for the runs. [2]

However, in October 2025, the migration in the Texas Hill Country has been stymied by unusually high temperatures. This heatwave, described as a persistent 'heat dome,' has resulted in far fewer sightings than normal during the expected peak. A recent scientific study suggests that such high temperatures can cause monarchs to enter a reproductive phase instead of migrating, as they lack the energy for both. This document serves as a practical guide for local planners, communities, and partners to integrate wildlife habitat connectivity into land use decisions. The report is part of a broader push to conserve wildlife corridors and features sample policies, case studies of successful implementation, and best practices to support local action. This initiative aims to address challenges like development pressure and preserve vital ecosystems by empowering local governments, which have land use authority over nearly two-thirds of the land in the U.S. The guide supports the protection of migratory routes for species such as pronghorn, elk, and mule deer through state and federal initiatives. <7> On the night of September 25, 2025, a record-breaking bird migration was detected over the United States by BirdCast, a collaborative research project.
